## Why this document exists

This package set out to fill a real, verifiable gap: at the time this
project started, no actively-maintained, CRAN-available package offered
`ggplot2`-native mosaic plots with statistical (residual-based) shading.
The original `ggmosaic` package had no shading support at all and was
archived in late 2025. Base R's `mosaicplot(shade = TRUE)` and the
`vcd`/`vcdExtra` packages have shading, but are base-graphics, not
grammar-of-graphics layers.

Partway through this project, a new package -- **`ggmosaic2`** (Michael
Friendly, with the original `ggmosaic` authors credited as co-authors),
published to CRAN on 2026-09-16 -- closed much of that gap directly,
including full n-way support. That is worth stating plainly rather than
talking around: as a *production recommendation today*, `ggmosaic2` is the
more complete package. This document exists to be honest about that, and to
state exactly what is and isn't still different about this package, based
on first-hand inspection of `ggmosaic2`'s source.

## Feature-by-feature comparison

| | Base R `mosaicplot()` | `ggmosaic2` (CRAN) | `mosaicresid` |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Input** | pre-built `table()` only | raw data + `aes(x = product(...))` | raw **or** pre-aggregated data, plain `aes(x =, y =)` |
| **API idiom** | base graphics function call | `product()`-wrapped `ggplot2` aes | plain `ggplot2` aes, no wrapper |
| **n-way support** | `margin` (loglinear model choice) | full, via `glm(poisson)` + formula/shortcut `expected =` | none -- explicit 2-way scope cut (see below) |
| **Residual types** | pearson / deviance / FT | pearson only | pearson / deviance / FT (matches base R exactly) |
| **Split direction** | `dir` override | `divider` (vspine/hspine/vbar/hbar -- 4 options) | `dir` override (v/h -- 2 options, a subset of their 4) |
| **Default color scale** | discrete HSV bins | continuous `scale_fill_gradient2()` | continuous `scale_fill_gradient2()` -- same design choice, arrived at independently |
| **Labels** | axis-side, fixed position | `ggrepel`-based collision handling | in-tile, size-threshold suppression |
| **Composability** | none (base graphics) | full `ggplot2` (facets, themes, `+`) | full `ggplot2` (facets, themes, `+`) |
| **Codebase** | 1 file, base R | ~3,500 lines, 20 files, 6 dependencies | 1 purpose, ~9 files, 4 dependencies |
| **Extras** | -- | `facet_mosaic()`, plotly export, Shiny app | tidy intermediate output (`compute_mosaic_residuals()` returns an inspectable data frame) |

## Is `aes(x =, y =)` vs `product()` a real differentiator?

Yes, but as a trade-off, not an unqualified win.

`ggplot2` only exposes two position-aesthetic slots. `ggmosaic2`'s
`product()` exists specifically to pack an arbitrary-length variable list
into the single `x` slot, so one interface scales from 1 variable up to n
(plus `conds` for conditioning variables). `mosaicresid`'s plain
`aes(x =, y =)` is more idiomatic -- it reads like every other `ggplot2`
geom, with no wrapper function to learn -- but that simplicity is purchased
by being two-variable-only. It would not generalize past two variables
without introducing something `product()`-shaped of its own. The API
difference and the n-way gap are, underneath, the same architectural
decision, not two independent facts.

So: a genuine, statable differentiator for the common two-variable case,
not a categorical advantage.

## Defending the one deliberate gap: n-way support

This is the only gap left unclosed by design, rather than by oversight.
Past two variables, "expected count" stops having a single unambiguous
definition -- complete independence, joint independence, conditional
independence, and all-two-way-associations are different, non-equivalent
loglinear models, and the caller has to choose one. `mosaicresid` ships a
narrow, well-defined two-way implementation, verified to floating-point
precision against base R's own residual formulas (see the package's test
suite, `tests/testthat/test-residuals.R`), with an explicit error that
fails loudly rather than silently computing a plausible-looking but wrong
number for an ambiguous n-way case -- naming `stats::loglin()` and
`glm(family = poisson)` as the path forward. `ggmosaic2` ended up shipping
exactly that `glm(family = poisson)` approach for its n-way support, which
is a reasonable outside confirmation that the scoping judgment here was
architecturally correct, even though this package doesn't implement it.

## Everything else: closed

Every other mechanical gap identified during development has been closed
and verified:

- **`dir`** (split direction override) -- implemented, matches base R's
  default alternating behavior when unset, and verified to correctly swap
  split roles when overridden.
- **`type`** (pearson / deviance / Freeman-Tukey residuals) -- implemented
  using base R's own formulas (read directly from
  `graphics:::mosaicplot.default`), verified to match base R to
  floating-point precision for all three.
- **`sort`** -- turned out not to be a real gap once examined. Base R needs
  `sort` because `x` is a fixed pre-built table; this package's
  `aes(x =, y =)` mapping *is* the permutation mechanism base R's `sort`
  provides after the fact -- swap which variable is `x` and which is `y`
  to get the same effect, with no separate parameter needed.

## Bottom line

`ggmosaic2` is the more feature-complete package, and is the right choice
for someone who needs n-way support, `ggrepel`-based label collision
handling, or a Shiny app, in production, today. `mosaicresid` matches or
exceeds it on the specific two-way, residual-shaded surface -- all three
residual types where `ggmosaic2` has one, verified to base R's own formulas
to the last bit -- with a simpler API and a fraction of the code, and
remains a legitimate, from-scratch statement of what true mosaic-plot
geometry and independence-residual shading look like as a `ggplot2` layer.
